name: Pashupatinath Temple
summary: Nepal’s foremost Shiva temple on the Bagmati — a UNESCO-linked sacred landscape and a living bridge between Himalayan Shaivism and Indian pilgrimage.
mythology: Pashupatinath in Kathmandu is Nepal’s foremost Shiva temple. Pashupati — ‘Lord of Beings’ — is an ancient form of Shiva celebrated in Himalayan and pan-Indian Shaiva devotion. The Bagmati riverside complex is a major cremation and pilgrimage landscape.
scriptureLinks: Accounts summarised from widely cited Puranic, epic, and pilgrimage traditions; local tellings may differ.
bestTime: October–March. Shivaratri needs lodging booked far ahead.
whatToCarry: Modest clothes, cash for offerings, passport/visa docs, scarf for temple norms.
climate: Valley climate — cool winters, warm summers, monsoon mid-year.
nearestRail: No direct Indian rail to Kathmandu; common route via Raxaul–Birgunj or flights.
accommodation: Hotels across Kathmandu; guesthouses near Thamel and airport corridor.
localFood: Newari and Nepali vegetarian thalis, temple-area snacks; sattvic options common for pilgrims.
otherFood: Kathmandu offers global cuisine away from the temple core.
localLanguage: Nepali; Hindi widely understood; English in tourist areas.
dressCode: Modest dress. Non-Hindus may face entry limits to the main sanctum — follow posted rules and guides.
darshanTimings: Early morning to evening with ritual breaks; confirm locally especially on festival days.
specialEntry: Security and queue systems intensify on Shivaratri; use official/local guidance only.
restrictions: Photography restricted in inner areas. Respect cremation ghats — no intrusive filming.
lockers: Bag rules vary; travel light inside the complex.
videoNote: Orientation videos — verify entry rules for international visitors.

mythologySignificance:
Pashupatinath in Kathmandu is Nepal’s foremost Shiva temple. Pashupati — ‘Lord of Beings’ — is an ancient form of Shiva celebrated in Himalayan and pan-Indian Shaiva devotion. The Bagmati riverside complex is a major cremation and pilgrimage landscape.

Pilgrimage literature treats Pashupatinath Temple as a tirtha — a crossing where devotion to Lord Shiva (Pashupati) is believed to bear fruit more readily than in ordinary space. Accounts summarised here follow widely cited epic, Puranic, and regional mahatmya traditions; temple priests remain the guides for ritual detail.
localBeliefs:
Shivaratri draws Himalayan and Indian pilgrims in vast numbers. Local Newar and Nepali traditions maintain distinctive ritual calendars around the shrine.

Proximity to Guhyeshwari Shakti Peetha creates a paired Shiva–Shakti belief for many Kathmandu valley devotees.

First-time visitors often hear several versions of the same story from pandas, taxi guides, and elderly pilgrims — a reminder that local belief is living conversation, not a single fixed text.
